title: Deep Time: Then and Now
learningObjectives: Order key developments in understanding geologic time from Steno to Patterson.
Explain how relative-time principles allow ordering of rock layers without absolute ages.
Describe how radioactivity provided a tool for absolute dating of Earth materials.

evidence.quote: The law of superposition says that older rocks are on the bottom and younger rocks are on the top.
allow observers to put geologic events in order to tell the story of relative time, but they don’t provide an absolute age.

explanations.text: Stratigraphic laws let observers order rock layers by relative position without giving a numerical age.

evidence.quote: the processes that we see happening on Earth today are the same processes that shaped Earth in the past
no vestige of a beginning. No prospect of an end.

explanations.text: Hutton argued that slow processes seen today built vast rocks in the past, implying enormously long geologic time.

evidence.quote: Radioactive decay solved the heat-flow question
and gave us a tool for measuring time.

explanations.text: Radioactivity explained Earth's heat and gave geologists a clock to measure absolute ages.

evidence.quote: Nicholas Steno, 1669, gets credit for first writing down basic geological principles as laws.
In 1788, James Hutton proposed what would become the foundational principle of geology — uniformitarianism.
In 1815, Smith developed the law of faunal succession, which states that species become extinct and are replaced by new species,
The first geologic time scale was published in 1841 — Powell certainly would have known of it and used it in his geologic trips to the West.
It was the discovery of radioactivity in 1896 that changed the heat-flow picture dramatically.
It was 1956 when Clair Cameron Patterson, an American geochemist, used lead-lead dating to determine that the Canyon Diablo meteorite was 4.55 billion
